input.project_name: Omnichannel Retail Order Hub
input.brd_text: Objective: unify online, mobile-app, and store orders in one operational view. Scope: order capture, inventory reservation, split shipments, cancellation rules, refunds, store pickup, customer notifications, and exception dashboards. Integrations: existing e-commerce storefront, ERP, warehouse management, payment gateway, courier APIs, and CRM. Data: migrate open orders and product-location inventory; retain historical order references for service agents. Non-functional needs: 99.9% availability, 18,000 orders/day, payment-data controls, and near-real-time stock updates. Rollout: pilot in 8 stores, then 120 stores.

real_life_risks: R1 [High | Integration dependencies] In UAT, messages between existing e-commerce storefront and ERP arrive late or twice, causing duplicate updates and stale records in Omnichannel Retail Order Hub that business testers cannot reconcile by hand. Indicative impact if unmanaged: 1–2 weeks of delay.

R2 [High | Availability & performance] A failover test two weeks before go-live shows that recovery of Omnichannel Retail Order Hub takes far longer than the agreed objectives, and the infrastructure team needs another environment cycle to fix it. Indicative impact if unmanaged: 1–2 weeks of delay.

R3 [Medium | Real-time processing] A downstream outage in Omnichannel Retail Order Hub causes messages to pile up, and the replay after recovery overwrites newer data with older data. Indicative impact if unmanaged: 1–2 weeks of delay.

R4 [Medium | Payments, billing & reconciliation] Orders or invoices in Omnichannel Retail Order Hub are posted twice or not at all after a timeout between systems, and finance spends weeks reconciling differences by hand. Indicative impact if unmanaged: 1–2 weeks of delay.

R5 [Medium | Phased rollout & coexistence] Each wave of Omnichannel Retail Order Hub needs its own data load, access set-up and support cover, and a delay in one wave pushes the others and stretches the team's time on the project. Indicative impact if unmanaged: 1–2 weeks of delay.
risk_mitigation: M1 (Integration dependencies): Agree interface contracts and test accounts for each of the 6 integrations in the first sprints, build contract tests plus mocks so work is not blocked, and name one accountable owner per interface with a response-time agreement.

M2 (Availability & performance): Run load tests at 1.5x expected peak with production-like data volumes, set performance budgets for key screens and integrations, and fix hotspots before UAT rather than after go-live.
M3 (Real-time processing): Use buffering with back-pressure, define what happens during outages, and replay with version checks.
M4 (Payments, billing & reconciliation): Test tax, rounding and currency rules with finance-approved scenarios and add automated daily reconciliation reports with exception queues.
M5 (Phased rollout & coexistence): Plan waves with fixed capacity for data load, access and support, keep a standing wave-readiness review, and protect the team from overlapping waves.
duration_reasoning: The model estimates 24 weeks (about 5.5 months) with a peak team of 16: 6 developers, 3 QA, 2 business analysts, 2 infrastructure, plus 1 project manager, 1 solution architect and 1 delivery lead. Indicative phase split (phases overlap in practice; the split sums to 24): discovery and design 3, build and configuration 8, integration and data work 5, testing and UAT 5, cutover and hypercare 3. Time drivers: (1) connecting existing e-commerce storefront, ERP and warehouse management means 6 interfaces that must each be specified, built against third-party schedules and tested end to end; (2) meeting 99.9% availability for the business users adds performance tuning cycles that sit in the test phase; (3) real-time updates need extra engineering and test effort compared to batch processing. Staffing rationale: 6 developers cover 8 scope areas (for example order capture and inventory reservation) and 6 integrations; the pool is moderate because the scope offers limited parallel streams. 3 QA engineers are sized for end-to-end integration regression. 2 infrastructure engineers handle environments, the 99.9% availability target, data-load runs and cutover support. Schedule sensitivity: if the 'Integration dependencies' risk is not contained, 1–2 weeks of slippage is realistic, so it is reviewed weekly.

input.project_name: Community Clinic Patient Portal
input.brd_text: Objective: let patients manage routine clinic interactions without calling reception. Scope: account registration, appointment booking and rescheduling, visit instructions, secure lab-result viewing, consent capture, and reminders. Integrations: existing practice-management system, SMS/email provider, and laboratory results service. Data: migrate portal account mappings only; clinical records remain in the source system. Indicative impact if unmanaged: 1–2 weeks of delay.

R2 [Medium | Scope growth] The BRD for Community Clinic Patient Portal is signed off at a high level, but during design workshops different departments interpret account registration differently, and rework is discovered only in UAT. Indicative impact if unmanaged: 1–2 weeks of delay.

R3 [Medium | Data migration] During the second trial load of the in-scope records from the legacy sources, a share of them fail mapping because of orphaned parent IDs and conflicting duplicates, so Community Clinic Patient Portal cannot be signed off for UAT on the planned date. Indicative impact if unmanaged: 1–2 weeks of delay.

R4 [Medium | Phased rollout & coexistence] Each wave of Community Clinic Patient Portal needs its own data load, access set-up and support cover, and a delay in one wave pushes the others and stretches the team's time on the project. Indicative impact if unmanaged: 1–2 weeks of delay.

R5 [Low | External users & partners] External partners or customers using Community Clinic Patient Portal register in unexpected ways (shared accounts, duplicate companies), and support spends time on access and identity problems instead of real issues. Indicative impact if unmanaged: 1–2 weeks of delay.

M2 (Scope growth): Reserve a small contingency (about 10%) for approved changes only and let the delivery lead publish a visible scope-versus-capacity burn-up each fortnight.

M3 (Data migration): Migrate in prioritised waves (open items first, history last), keep the source system read-only but reachable for a fixed period, and publish a daily load-quality scorecard to the business owners.
M4 (Phased rollout & coexistence): Plan waves with fixed capacity for data load, access and support, keep a standing wave-readiness review, and protect the team from overlapping waves.

M5 (External users & partners): Design an onboarding and verification flow for external users, test tenant isolation with explicit cross-partner cases, and provide self-service password and access help.

Indicative phase split (phases overlap in practice; the split sums to 16): discovery and design 2, build and configuration 5, integration and data work 4, testing and UAT 3, cutover and hypercare 2. In-scope capabilities include assignment inbox, offline forms, barcode/photo capture, digital sign-off, rescheduling and conflict resolution. The service is built on a .NET service layer with a React web client and serves analysts and managers who reconcile operational exceptions. Integration dependencies: work-order system, GIS, identity, push notifications and device management. Data conversion is limited to an agreed scope: reconcile transactional events by date and status, with business owners signing off exceptions before cutover. Access and assurance requirements include consent-aware processing, searchable access history and a formal review for bulk data extraction; service operations must ensure that the system must provide operational telemetry, actionable alert thresholds and a tested rollback path. Scale assumptions cover a blend of mobile field users, supervisors and back-office support functions. Release strategy: a single-region launch with localization and additional integrations delivered later. Go-live is blocked until reconciliation thresholds, restore tests and critical defect exit criteria are met. The team will evaluate results using baseline and target measures include cycle time, first-contact resolution, exception rate and user adoption. The initiative emphasizes ai-assisted processing with human approval. For the wholesale distribution operating model, the team must confirm data owners, exception handling and local support responsibilities.

real_life_risks: R1 [High | Integration dependencies] The 5 planned interfaces (work-order system, GIS and identity) are owned by different teams; the owner of work-order system changes an API contract two weeks before UAT and the nightly sync for Mobile field-work management application for Wholesale distribution starts failing without a clear owner. Indicative impact if unmanaged: 1–3 weeks of delay.

R2 [High | Offline use & data sync] A new phone model or operating-system update breaks the offline cache of Mobile field-work management application for Wholesale distribution, and technicians lose a day of captured photos and notes. Indicative impact if unmanaged: 1–3 weeks of delay.

R3 [High | AI answer quality & knowledge] Usage costs and response times of the AI components in Mobile field-work management application for Wholesale distribution grow faster than expected after launch, forcing a late redesign of prompts and caching. Indicative impact if unmanaged: 1–3 weeks of delay.

R4 [Medium | Real-time processing] A downstream outage in Mobile field-work management application for Wholesale distribution causes messages to pile up, and the replay after recovery overwrites newer data with older data. Indicative impact if unmanaged: 1–3 weeks of delay.

R5 [Medium | Data migration] After go-live of the pilot group, users of Mobile field-work management application for Wholesale distribution find historical records missing or attached to the wrong customer, because the conversion of the in-scope records from the legacy sources was only checked on a sample. Indicative impact if unmanaged: 1–3 weeks of delay.
risk_mitigation: M1 (Integration dependencies): Make every interface idempotent with retry and dead-letter handling, add integration monitoring that alerts on lag or failures, and schedule a joint end-to-end test with work-order system and GIS before UAT begins.
M2 (Offline use & data sync): Define explicit conflict-resolution rules, test sync on throttled and intermittent networks, and keep payloads small by syncing only what each role needs.
M3 (AI answer quality & knowledge): Add cost and latency budgets, caching and a fallback to non-AI search, and release the AI feature to a small group first with monitoring.
M4 (Real-time processing): Use buffering with back-pressure, define what happens during outages, and replay with version checks.

M5 (Data migration): Profile and cleanse the legacy sources before build starts, run at least three timed trial loads with record-count and field-level reconciliation, and give a named data steward the authority to resolve conflicts within 48 hours.

Indicative phase split (phases overlap in practice; the split sums to 27): discovery and design 3, build and configuration 9, integration and data work 6, testing and UAT 6, cutover and hypercare 3. Time drivers: (1) connecting work-order system, GIS and identity means 5 interfaces that must each be specified, built against third-party schedules and tested end to end; (2) mobile and offline use adds test cycles for sync, devices and poor connectivity; (3) the assistant/knowledge capability adds quality-evaluation iterations that cannot be skipped before release. Staffing rationale: 10 developers cover 6 scope areas (for example assignment inbox and offline forms) and 5 integrations; this is a larger pool because the work splits into parallel streams. 4 QA engineers are sized for reconciliation checks, device and sync testing and end-to-end integration regression. 1 infrastructure engineer handle environments, data-load runs and cutover support. Functional scope includes membership lifecycle, tier rules, points/benefits visibility, service recovery cases, member communications and audit reports. Primary users are citizens or customers using authenticated self-service channels, and the solution must support approximately 150–300 named users across the initial operating group. Platform approach: implement on a custom CRM product on a cloud-native application stack. Core integration dependencies include loyalty engine, POS/commerce, marketing automation, payment and identity; transactional ownership remains with the designated source systems. Data transition: reconcile transactional events by date and status, with business owners signing off exceptions before cutover. Non-functional and control requirements include accessible user flows, privacy-by-design defaults and auditable changes to customer permissions; the platform must support regional business hours, multilingual content and accessible keyboard navigation. Delivery plan: a staged cloud cutover that keeps the previous service available for an agreed rollback window. Business readiness requires that post-launch measurement tracks adoption, failure rate, cycle time and open defects against an agreed baseline. Acceptance measures: the launch dashboard compares adoption, workflow completion, customer effort and control failures against baseline. Delivery emphasis: Customer identity and consent alignment. Industry context: Air transport; the design must reflect strict identity verification, burst handling during disruptions and controlled access to traveler data.

real_life_risks: R1 [Medium | User adoption & training] Training for Loyalty and membership engagement CRM for Air transport is scheduled before the final design settles, so users learn screens that later change, and the service desk is flooded with how-do-I tickets in week one. Indicative impact if unmanaged: 1–2 weeks of delay.

R2 [Medium | Custom-build complexity] Because Loyalty and membership engagement CRM for Air transport is built on the custom platform, common functions (audit trail, permissions, scheduling) have to be built from scratch and take longer than the estimates, squeezing testing time. Indicative impact if unmanaged: 1–2 weeks of delay.

R3 [Low | External users & partners] External partners or customers using Loyalty and membership engagement CRM for Air transport register in unexpected ways (shared accounts, duplicate companies), and support spends time on access and identity problems instead of real issues. Indicative impact if unmanaged: 1–2 weeks of delay.

R4 [Low | Stakeholder decisions & approvals] A key approver for Loyalty and membership engagement CRM for Air transport is unavailable during the design sign-off window, so build starts on unapproved assumptions that are later reversed. Indicative impact if unmanaged: 1–2 weeks of delay.
risk_mitigation: M1 (User adoption & training): Track adoption KPIs (active users, records created, old-tool usage) weekly after go-live, and have leaders review them in team meetings until usage stabilises.
M2 (Custom-build complexity): Set architectural guardrails with the solution architect and run code reviews that check design conformance.
M3 (External users & partners): Run a closed beta with a few friendly partners, collect feedback, and publish known issues before wider launch.
M4 (Stakeholder decisions & approvals): Schedule sign-off windows at kick-off and protect them in stakeholder calendars.
duration_reasoning: The model estimates 12 weeks (about 2.8 months) with a peak team of 8: 2 developers, 1 QA, 1 business analyst, 1 infrastructure, plus 1 project manager, 1 solution architect and 1 delivery lead. Indicative phase split (phases overlap in practice; the split sums to 12): discovery and design 2, build and configuration 4, integration and data work 2, testing and UAT 2, cutover and hypercare 2. Time drivers: (1) moving 150–300 named users onto Loyalty and membership engagement CRM for Air transport requires training, champion support and a stabilisation period after go-live; (2) the custom platform adds build and test effort that configurable products would avoid; (3) partner/portal use requires isolation testing and onboarding flows that internal-only systems avoid. Staffing rationale: 2 developers cover 6 scope areas (for example membership lifecycle and tier rules); the pool is moderate because the scope offers limited parallel streams. 1 QA engineer are sized for control and compliance evidence and reconciliation checks. 1 infrastructure engineer handle environments, cutover support. Schedule sensitivity: if the 'User adoption & training' risk is not contained, 1–2 weeks of slippage is realistic, so it is reviewed weekly.

Non-functional and control requirements include accessible user flows, privacy-by-design defaults and auditable changes to customer permissions; peak load is expected around monthly close; batch workloads must finish within the business reporting window. Delivery plan: a minimum viable release followed by prioritized enhancements over two release trains. Business readiness requires that the first release must coexist with existing reporting until users validate the new metric definitions. Acceptance measures: success is measured through reduced manual rekeying, higher data completeness and faster exception resolution. Delivery emphasis: Release engineering and observability uplift. R2 [Medium | Phased rollout & coexistence] During the rollout of Media and entertainment Mobile field-work management application (a staged rollout), the old and new systems both hold live data; users in the first wave update one system while later waves use the other, and managers see two versions of the truth. R3 [Medium | Custom-build complexity] A shortcut taken to hit a milestone in Media and entertainment Mobile field-work management application becomes technical debt, and later changes to workflows require reworking several modules. Indicative impact if unmanaged: 1–2 weeks of delay.

The delivery scope covers account hierarchy, subscription amendments, plan-change requests, dunning handoff, renewal tasks and entitlement visibility. Users include security operations, platform engineering and service owners; the product must support roughly 500 concurrent users during peak business periods. Target architecture: Microsoft Dynamics 365 with Power Platform extensions. Upstream and downstream dependencies are subscription management, billing, identity service, payment gateway and product telemetry. Migration approach: migrate active records plus 24 months of high-value history, preserve source identifiers and reconcile counts by business unit. Controls include tenant and legal-entity isolation, encrypted data in transit and at rest, and monitored privileged access, while operations must ensure that interactive pages should remain responsive for a large concurrent user population and expose actionable errors. The business wants a service automation and escalation redesign and will release it through an incremental rollout with a hypercare rota and named business owners for each wave. Training and floor-walker support are required for the first two weeks after each deployment wave Measures for acceptance include operational scorecards cover availability, queue aging, completion time, failed integrations and cost per transaction. Industry context: Construction and engineering; the design must reflect contract-level permissions, document traceability and support for distributed field users.

real_life_risks: R1 [Medium | Key-person & skills dependency] A specialised skill needed for Construction and engineering Subscription account lifecycle CRM (for example configuration or integration work on Dynamics 365) is hard to recruit, and the planned start of that workstream slips by several weeks. Indicative impact if unmanaged: 1–3 weeks of delay.

R2 [Medium | Phased rollout & coexistence] The pilot of Construction and engineering Subscription account lifecycle CRM goes well, but lessons from it (changed fields, new validation rules) arrive after the next wave's training material is produced, so later groups receive outdated guidance. Indicative impact if unmanaged: 2–4 weeks of delay.

R3 [Medium | Payments, billing & reconciliation] A failed payment or refund callback leaves a transaction in an unknown state, and customers are charged without a matching order in Construction and engineering Subscription account lifecycle CRM. Indicative impact if unmanaged: 2–4 weeks of delay.

R4 [Low | User adoption & training] Training for Construction and engineering Subscription account lifecycle CRM is scheduled before the final design settles, so users learn screens that later change, and the service desk is flooded with how-do-I tickets in week one. Indicative impact if unmanaged: 1–3 weeks of delay.

R5 [Medium | Data migration] During the second trial load of the in-scope records from the legacy sources, a share of them fail mapping because of orphaned parent IDs and conflicting duplicates, so Construction and engineering Subscription account lifecycle CRM cannot be signed off for UAT on the planned date. Indicative impact if unmanaged: 2–4 weeks of delay.

R6 [Low | Identity & access mapping] Access groups are loaded after business data, so records in Construction and engineering Subscription account lifecycle CRM are visible to the wrong teams for several days. Indicative impact if unmanaged: 1–3 weeks of delay.
risk_mitigation: M1 (Key-person & skills dependency): Pair developers on critical components, keep design decisions in a shared log and code in a reviewed repository, and nominate a named backup for the architect and delivery lead.

M2 (Phased rollout & coexistence): Define which system is the source of truth per object for every wave, build a reconciliation report that runs daily during coexistence, and keep the coexistence period as short as the business accepts.

M3 (Payments, billing & reconciliation): Define the financial source of truth, make posting idempotent with unique transaction keys, and run parallel reconciliation with finance for at least one full close before go-live.
M4 (User adoption & training): Retire the old tools on a published date, collect early feedback through a short pulse survey, and fix the top friction points in a first post-go-live release.

M5 (Data migration): Migrate in prioritised waves (open items first, history last), keep the source system read-only but reachable for a fixed period, and publish a daily load-quality scorecard to the business owners.
M6 (Identity & access mapping): Validate the role matrix with business owners, load access groups before business data, and test with real user accounts (including contractors) before UAT.
duration_reasoning: The model estimates 39 weeks (about 9.0 months) with a peak team of 30: 12 developers, 5 QA, 6 business analysts, 2 infrastructure, plus 1 project manager, 3 solution architects and 1 delivery lead. Indicative phase split (phases overlap in practice; the split sums to 39): discovery and design 5, build and configuration 13, integration and data work 7, testing and UAT 8, cutover and hypercare 6. Time drivers: (1) the planned team (12 developers and 5 QA at peak) relies on specialised skills for Dynamics 365, so work cannot be compressed by adding people late; (2) the rollout approach (a phased rollout) means repeated readiness, data-load and support cycles after the first release, which extends the late-stage plan; (3) billing/payment flows add reconciliation testing that has to run on realistic cycles. Staffing rationale: 12 developers cover 6 scope areas (for example account hierarchy and subscription amendments); this is a larger pool because the work splits into parallel streams. 5 QA engineers are sized for reconciliation checks. 6 business analysts cover requirements and UAT scripting. Schedule sensitivity: if the 'Key-person & skills dependency' risk is not contained, 1–3 weeks of slippage is realistic, so it is reviewed weekly.

The delivery scope covers route planning, driver assignment, geofenced milestones, exception re-planning, proof of service and performance reports. Users include customer success, support and implementation managers; the product must support internal teams plus external partners using delegated, least-privilege access. Target architecture: a modular monolith with clear service boundaries and an automated release pipeline. Upstream and downstream dependencies are telematics, GIS, order management, mobile app and customer notifications. Migration approach: profile and cleanse contact, product and location data before loading; unresolved conflicts go to stewardship queues. Controls include secure API authentication, secrets rotation, rate limits and alerting for anomalous access patterns, while operations must ensure that bulk operations must be resumable, report partial failure clearly and preserve the source-to-target reconciliation trail. The business wants a security hardening and identity integration and will release it through an incremental rollout with a hypercare rota and named business owners for each wave. Release readiness includes accessibility review, operational runbooks, support knowledge and monitoring dashboards Measures for acceptance include success is measured through reduced manual rekeying, higher data completeness and faster exception resolution. Industry context: Public services; the design must reflect records-retention policy, accessibility, data minimization and auditable decisions.

real_life_risks: R1 [Medium | Device & telemetry reliability] Device identities and credentials for Fleet routing and dispatch optimization for Public services are provisioned by hand, and a few compromised or misconfigured devices are not detected. Indicative impact if unmanaged: 1–2 weeks of delay.

R2 [Medium | Data migration] During the second trial load of the in-scope records from the legacy sources, a share of them fail mapping because of orphaned parent IDs and conflicting duplicates, so Fleet routing and dispatch optimization for Public services cannot be signed off for UAT on the planned date. Indicative impact if unmanaged: 1–2 weeks of delay.

R3 [Low | Identity & access mapping] Single sign-on for Fleet routing and dispatch optimization for Public services works in test but fails for contractors and external users in production because their identities live in a different directory. Indicative impact if unmanaged: 1–2 weeks of delay.

R4 [Medium | Phased rollout & coexistence] The pilot of Fleet routing and dispatch optimization for Public services goes well, but lessons from it (changed fields, new validation rules) arrive after the next wave's training material is produced, so later groups receive outdated guidance. Indicative impact if unmanaged: 1–2 weeks of delay.

R5 [Medium | Payments, billing & reconciliation] Orders or invoices in Fleet routing and dispatch optimization for Public services are posted twice or not at all after a timeout between systems, and finance spends weeks reconciling differences by hand. Indicative impact if unmanaged: 1–2 weeks of delay.
risk_mitigation: M1 (Device & telemetry reliability): Normalise payloads at the edge of the platform, test with the real device and firmware mix, and tune alert thresholds in a supervised pilot period before alarms reach operators.

M2 (Data migration): Freeze the field mapping early, keep legacy external IDs on every migrated record, and block UAT entry until the trial-load reconciliation shows no unexplained variance on the agreed critical entities.
M3 (Identity & access mapping): Use a small set of well-defined roles, keep an emergency access procedure, and log every permission change.

M4 (Phased rollout & coexistence): Turn pilot lessons into a controlled change list reviewed before each wave, update training material from one maintained source, and use readiness checklists per wave as an entry gate.

M5 (Payments, billing & reconciliation): Define the financial source of truth, make posting idempotent with unique transaction keys, and run parallel reconciliation with finance for at least one full close before go-live.
duration_reasoning: The model estimates 19 weeks (about 4.4 months) with a peak team of 14: 6 developers, 2 QA, 1 business analyst, 2 infrastructure, plus 1 project manager, 1 solution architect and 1 delivery lead. Indicative phase split (phases overlap in practice; the split sums to 19): discovery and design 2, build and configuration 6, integration and data work 4, testing and UAT 4, cutover and hypercare 3. Time drivers: (1) telemetry volumes and device variety add ingestion design and tuning time; (2) the conversion of the in-scope records from the legacy sources cannot be rushed because every trial load must be reconciled before UAT can start; (3) access-model design adds early design effort and later verification time. Staffing rationale: 6 developers cover 6 scope areas (for example route planning and driver assignment); the pool is moderate because the scope offers limited parallel streams. 2 QA engineers are sized for control and compliance evidence and reconciliation checks. 1 business analyst cover external user journeys. Schedule sensitivity: if the 'Device & telemetry reliability' risk is not contained, 1–2 weeks of slippage is realistic, so it is reviewed weekly.

In-scope capabilities include channel ingestion, identity matching, moderation, case conversion, consent handling, response templates and audit reports. The service is built on HubSpot CRM with governed integrations and serves regional operations owners and product administrators. Integration dependencies: social listening provider, CRM service, contact center, content moderation and analytics. Data conversion is limited to an agreed scope: load reference data and access groups before business transactions, then validate ownership and permission mappings. Access and assurance requirements include consent-aware processing, searchable access history and a formal review for bulk data extraction; service operations must ensure that integration failures must retry safely, avoid duplicate business events and surface unresolved exceptions to owners. Scale assumptions cover a large customer-facing population with secure self-service and assisted-service journeys. Release strategy: a phased migration by legal entity, with rollback criteria at each cutover gate. Partner onboarding is staged so that support capacity and integration limits are validated before expansion. The team will evaluate results using operational scorecards cover availability, queue aging, completion time, failed integrations and cost per transaction. The initiative emphasizes omnichannel integration. Industry context: Insurance brokerage; the design must reflect audit-ready advice records, permission separation and secure document exchange.

real_life_risks: R1 [High | Integration dependencies] A sandbox for social listening provider is not available until halfway through the build, so Insurance brokerage Social engagement and digital case capture is developed against mocks and the first real end-to-end run exposes field-format and authentication problems. Indicative impact if unmanaged: 1–2 weeks of delay.

R2 [Medium | Phased rollout & coexistence] Each wave of Insurance brokerage Social engagement and digital case capture needs its own data load, access set-up and support cover, and a delay in one wave pushes the others and stretches the team's time on the project. Indicative impact if unmanaged: 1–2 weeks of delay.

R3 [Medium | Data quality & reporting trust] A source system changes a field format without notice and the nightly load into Insurance brokerage Social engagement and digital case capture silently drops rows for several days before anyone notices. Indicative impact if unmanaged: 1–2 weeks of delay.

R4 [Medium | Scope growth] Once business users see early demos of Insurance brokerage Social engagement and digital case capture, new requests appear around channel ingestion and identity matching; each looks small but together they push the backlog beyond what the sprint plan can absorb. Indicative impact if unmanaged: 1–2 weeks of delay.

R5 [Low | External users & partners] A partner sees data that belongs to another organisation because a sharing rule in Insurance brokerage Social engagement and digital case capture was too broad. Indicative impact if unmanaged: 1–2 weeks of delay.
risk_mitigation: M1 (Integration dependencies): Make every interface idempotent with retry and dead-letter handling, add integration monitoring that alerts on lag or failures, and schedule a joint end-to-end test with social listening provider and CRM service before UAT begins.
M2 (Phased rollout & coexistence): Plan waves with fixed capacity for data load, access and support, keep a standing wave-readiness review, and protect the team from overlapping waves.

M3 (Data quality & reporting trust): Agree one written definition per key metric with a named owner, put data contracts and automated quality checks on every feed, and reconcile dashboards to a trusted report before launch.

M4 (Scope growth): Baseline the scope with a prioritised (must/should/could) backlog, run a formal change-control board with impact estimates in weeks, and freeze scope for channel ingestion and the other core areas before build is 60% done.
M5 (External users & partners): Prepare partner communications and a support route in advance, and monitor activation rates after launch.
duration_reasoning: The model estimates 22 weeks (about 5.1 months) with a peak team of 14: 5 developers, 2 QA, 2 business analysts, 2 infrastructure, plus 1 project manager, 1 solution architect and 1 delivery lead. Indicative phase split (phases overlap in practice; the split sums to 22): discovery and design 3, build and configuration 7, integration and data work 5, testing and UAT 4, cutover and hypercare 3. Time drivers: (1) connecting social listening provider, CRM service and contact center means 5 interfaces that must each be specified, built against third-party schedules and tested end to end; (2) the rollout approach (a phased migration by legal entity, with rollback criteria at each cutover gate) means repeated readiness, data-load and support cycles after the first release, which extends the late-stage plan; (3) the reporting and data-unification scope depends on feed quality and metric agreement, which takes iterative reconciliation. Staffing rationale: 5 developers cover 7 scope areas (for example channel ingestion and identity matching) and 5 integrations; the pool is moderate because the scope offers limited parallel streams. 2 QA engineers are sized for control and compliance evidence and end-to-end integration regression. 2 infrastructure engineers handle environments, data-load runs and cutover support. Functional scope includes cost ingestion, allocation rules, forecast alerts, unit economics, recommendation workflow and monthly reconciliation. Primary users are sales operations, account owners and finance approvers, and the solution must support a distributed user base across 4–12 regions with separate local administrators. Platform approach: implement on a cloud-native web application with managed database services. Core integration dependencies include cloud billing APIs, CMDB, finance warehouse, identity and ticketing; transactional ownership remains with the designated source systems. Data transition: use staged mock migrations to validate relationships, duplicate handling, attachment links and reconciliation totals. Non-functional and control requirements include field-level protection for sensitive attributes, purpose-based access and reviewable export permissions; mobile workflows should tolerate intermittent connectivity and clearly resolve stale or conflicting updates. Delivery plan: an incremental rollout with a hypercare rota and named business owners for each wave. Business readiness requires that go-live is blocked until reconciliation thresholds, restore tests and critical defect exit criteria are met. Acceptance measures: the product owner will track transaction success, median response time, unresolved exceptions and support demand. Delivery emphasis: Data migration and reconciliation wave. The business users work in commercial banking, so ownership of customer and account references, consent records, interaction history and open cases must be agreed before configuration freeze.

real_life_risks: R1 [High | Offline use & data sync] Field users of Commercial banking Cloud cost management and FinOps dashboards work in basements and rural sites without signal; two people edit the same record offline, and on sync one change silently overwrites the other. Indicative impact if unmanaged: 2–4 weeks of delay.

R2 [High | AI answer quality & knowledge] In UAT the AI features of Commercial banking Cloud cost management and FinOps dashboards perform well on the demo script but poorly on real, messy requests, so business users lose trust and ask for the feature to be switched off. Indicative impact if unmanaged: 1–3 weeks of delay.

R3 [Medium | Data quality & reporting trust] The first dashboards of Commercial banking Cloud cost management and FinOps dashboards show numbers that differ from finance and operations reports, because source feeds are late or defined differently, and leaders stop trusting the data. Indicative impact if unmanaged: 1–3 weeks of delay.

R4 [Medium | Real-time processing] A traffic spike overloads the message broker behind Commercial banking Cloud cost management and FinOps dashboards, and delays turn near-real-time updates into updates that arrive minutes late. Indicative impact if unmanaged: 1–3 weeks of delay.

R5 [Medium | Custom-build complexity] A shortcut taken to hit a milestone in Commercial banking Cloud cost management and FinOps dashboards becomes technical debt, and later changes to workflows require reworking several modules. Indicative impact if unmanaged: 1–3 weeks of delay.

R6 [Medium | Data migration] After go-live of the pilot group, users of Commercial banking Cloud cost management and FinOps dashboards find historical records missing or attached to the wrong customer, because the conversion of the in-scope records from the legacy sources was only checked on a sample. Indicative impact if unmanaged: 2–4 weeks of delay.
risk_mitigation: M1 (Offline use & data sync): Publish a supported-device matrix, run a field pilot with real connectivity conditions before the full release, and include a safe recovery path for local data that failed to upload.

M2 (AI answer quality & knowledge): Assign owners and review dates for every knowledge article, add a feedback button on each answer, and measure resolution and escalation rates rather than demo performance.

M3 (Data quality & reporting trust): Agree one written definition per key metric with a named owner, put data contracts and automated quality checks on every feed, and reconcile dashboards to a trusted report before launch.
M4 (Real-time processing): Design for ordering and idempotency (event versions, de-duplication keys), load-test spikes, and monitor end-to-end latency with alerts.
M5 (Custom-build complexity): Write handover documentation and runbooks as part of Definition of Done for each component.

M6 (Data migration): Freeze the field mapping early, keep legacy external IDs on every migrated record, and block UAT entry until the trial-load reconciliation shows no unexplained variance on the agreed critical entities.

Indicative phase split (phases overlap in practice; the split sums to 37): discovery and design 4, build and configuration 13, integration and data work 8, testing and UAT 8, cutover and hypercare 4. Time drivers: (1) mobile and offline use adds test cycles for sync, devices and poor connectivity; (2) AI and knowledge features need an evaluation set, content clean-up and tuning cycles that run alongside normal build work; (3) the reporting and data-unification scope depends on feed quality and metric agreement, which takes iterative reconciliation. Staffing rationale: 9 developers cover 6 scope areas (for example cost ingestion and allocation rules); this is a larger pool because the work splits into parallel streams. 4 QA engineers are sized for reconciliation checks and device and sync testing. 3 business analysts cover requirements and UAT scripting. Schedule sensitivity: if the 'Offline use & data sync' risk is not contained, 2–4 weeks of slippage is realistic, so it is reviewed weekly.

The delivery scope covers template selection, signer routing, identity checks, callback validation, completed-document storage and audit reports. Users include front-line service teams and their supervisors; the product must support a large customer-facing population with secure self-service and assisted-service journeys. Target architecture: a serverless workflow and API architecture. Upstream and downstream dependencies are CLM, CRM, ERP, identity provider and records management. Migration approach: profile and cleanse contact, product and location data before loading; unresolved conflicts go to stewardship queues. Controls include tenant and legal-entity isolation, encrypted data in transit and at rest, and monitored privileged access, while operations must ensure that planned maintenance must be visible to users and critical workflows must degrade safely if a dependency is unavailable. The business wants a ai-assisted processing with human approval and will release it through an initial release for a limited user cohort followed by monthly rollout waves. The delivery team must demonstrate audit evidence and role-based access in user acceptance testing Measures for acceptance include operational scorecards cover availability, queue aging, completion time, failed integrations and cost per transaction. For the financial technology operating model, the team must confirm data owners, exception handling and local support responsibilities.

real_life_risks: R1 [Medium | AI answer quality & knowledge] Usage costs and response times of the AI components in Financial technology E-signature and contract workflow integration grow faster than expected after launch, forcing a late redesign of prompts and caching. Indicative impact if unmanaged: 1–2 weeks of delay.

R2 [Low | Identity & access mapping] Access groups are loaded after business data, so records in Financial technology E-signature and contract workflow integration are visible to the wrong teams for several days. Indicative impact if unmanaged: 1–2 weeks of delay.

R3 [Medium | Phased rollout & coexistence] During the rollout of Financial technology E-signature and contract workflow integration (a phased rollout), the old and new systems both hold live data; users in the first wave update one system while later waves use the other, and managers see two versions of the truth. Indicative impact if unmanaged: 1–2 weeks of delay.

R4 [Low | External users & partners] External partners or customers using Financial technology E-signature and contract workflow integration register in unexpected ways (shared accounts, duplicate companies), and support spends time on access and identity problems instead of real issues. Indicative impact if unmanaged: 1–2 weeks of delay.

R5 [Medium | Data migration] During the second trial load of the in-scope records from the legacy sources, a share of them fail mapping because of orphaned parent IDs and conflicting duplicates, so Financial technology E-signature and contract workflow integration cannot be signed off for UAT on the planned date. Indicative impact if unmanaged: 1–2 weeks of delay.
risk_mitigation: M1 (AI answer quality & knowledge): Ground answers on approved content with source references, build an evaluation set of real requests that must pass a quality threshold before each release, and keep a human review step for high-impact outputs.
M2 (Identity & access mapping): Automate joiner-mover-leaver provisioning from the identity source and run an access review one month after go-live.

M3 (Phased rollout & coexistence): Turn pilot lessons into a controlled change list reviewed before each wave, update training material from one maintained source, and use readiness checklists per wave as an entry gate.

M4 (External users & partners): Design an onboarding and verification flow for external users, test tenant isolation with explicit cross-partner cases, and provide self-service password and access help.

M5 (Data migration): Profile and cleanse the legacy sources before build starts, run at least three timed trial loads with record-count and field-level reconciliation, and give a named data steward the authority to resolve conflicts within 48 hours.

Indicative phase split (phases overlap in practice; the split sums to 21): discovery and design 2, build and configuration 8, integration and data work 4, testing and UAT 4, cutover and hypercare 3. R2 [Medium | Data quality & reporting trust] A source system changes a field format without notice and the nightly load into Commercial banking Customer 360 and master-data unification silently drops rows for several days before anyone notices. Indicative impact if unmanaged: 1–2 weeks of delay.

Scope: golden record views; match and merge rules; duplicate detection; security scanning; automated tests; operational runbooks; model-driven dashboards; audit history. Integrations: legacy CRM. Data: migrate about 317,000 records from an ERP customer table. Non-functional needs: performance for 296 named users, 99.5% availability target; public records retention rules. Rollout: a single cutover weekend.

real_life_risks: R1 [High | Data migration] After go-live of the pilot group, users of Logistics and freight - customer 360 data unification find historical records missing or attached to the wrong customer, because the conversion of 317,000 records from ERP customer table was only checked on a sample. Indicative impact if unmanaged: 1–2 weeks of delay.

R2 [High | Big-bang cutover] The go/no-go meeting for Logistics and freight - customer 360 data unification is held under pressure with open severity-2 defects, and the decision to proceed is later regretted when workarounds overwhelm the support desk. R3 [Medium | Data quality & reporting trust] Two departments argue over the definition of a key measure in Logistics and freight - customer 360 data unification, so metric sign-off is delayed and dashboards are rebuilt twice. Indicative impact if unmanaged: 1–2 weeks of delay.

R4 [Medium | Availability & performance] On the first peak day, Logistics and freight - customer 360 data unification slows down for 296 named users because queries and integrations were only tested with a fraction of the real volume, and the 99.5% availability target is missed. Indicative phase split (phases overlap in practice; the split sums to 11): discovery and design 1, build and configuration 3, integration and data work 3, testing and UAT 2, cutover and hypercare 2. Time drivers: (1) moving 317,000 records from ERP customer table needs profiling, mapping, cleansing and repeated trial loads, which is why the data work takes roughly 3 weeks of the plan; (2) the all-at-once cutover requires more rehearsal and stabilisation weeks than a staged rollout would; (3) the reporting and data-unification scope depends on feed quality and metric agreement, which takes iterative reconciliation. Scope: delegation; SLA clock; approval limits; Teams or Outlook notifications. Integrations: HR information system, payment gateway, e-signature service, document management system. Data: migrate about 26,000 records from spreadsheets. Non-functional needs: performance for 637 named users, 99.9% availability target; segregation of duties for approvals, SOX audit trail. Rollout: a single cutover weekend.

real_life_risks: R1 [High | Big-bang cutover] A defect found in the first hour after cutover of Retail banking - approval workflow automation cannot be fixed quickly, and because there is no pilot group the whole user base is affected at once. Indicative impact if unmanaged: 1–2 weeks of delay.

R2 [High | Data migration] After go-live of the pilot group, users of Retail banking - approval workflow automation find historical records missing or attached to the wrong customer, because the conversion of 26,000 records from spreadsheets was only checked on a sample. Indicative impact if unmanaged: 1–2 weeks of delay.

R3 [High | Availability & performance] A failover test two weeks before go-live shows that recovery of Retail banking - approval workflow automation takes far longer than the agreed objectives, and the infrastructure team needs another environment cycle to fix it. Indicative impact if unmanaged: 1–2 weeks of delay.

R4 [High | Integration dependencies] The 4 planned interfaces (HR information system, payment gateway and e-signature service) are owned by different teams; the owner of HR information system changes an API contract two weeks before UAT and the nightly sync for Retail banking - approval workflow automation starts failing without a clear owner. Indicative impact if unmanaged: 1–2 weeks of delay.
risk_mitigation: M1 (Big-bang cutover): Hold at least two full dress rehearsals with timings, define a written rollback point and rollback test, and agree measurable go/no-go criteria with the business owner two weeks ahead.

M2 (Data migration): Freeze the field mapping early, keep legacy external IDs on every migrated record, and block UAT entry until the trial-load reconciliation shows no unexplained variance on the agreed critical entities.

M3 (Availability & performance): Rehearse failover and restore at least once, document recovery objectives and runbooks, and add monitoring with alerting thresholds tied to the 99.9% availability target.

M4 (Integration dependencies): Agree interface contracts and test accounts for each of the 4 integrations in the first sprints, build contract tests plus mocks so work is not blocked, and name one accountable owner per interface with a response-time agreement.
duration_reasoning: The model estimates 13 weeks (about 3.0 months) with a peak team of 13: 5 developers, 2 QA, 2 business analysts, 1 infrastructure, plus 1 project manager, 1 solution architect and 1 delivery lead. Indicative phase split (phases overlap in practice; the split sums to 13): discovery and design 1, build and configuration 4, integration and data work 3, testing and UAT 3, cutover and hypercare 2. Time drivers: (1) the all-at-once cutover requires more rehearsal and stabilisation weeks than a staged rollout would; (2) the conversion of 26,000 records from spreadsheets cannot be rushed because every trial load must be reconciled before UAT can start; (3) meeting 99.9% availability for 637 named users adds performance tuning cycles that sit in the test phase. Staffing rationale: 5 developers cover 4 scope areas (for example delegation and SLA clock) and 4 integrations; the pool is moderate because the scope offers limited parallel streams. 2 QA engineers are sized for control and compliance evidence and end-to-end integration regression. 1 infrastructure engineer handle environments, the 99.9% availability target, data-load runs and cutover support. Scope: review workflow; search analytics; environment variables and connection references; Power Automate notifications; audit history. Integrations: knowledge base, e-commerce platform, telephony platform, legacy CRM, SMS gateway, billing platform. Data: migrate about 32,000 records from an older Dynamics 365 instance. Non-functional needs: performance for 709 named users, 99.9% availability target; SOX audit trail. Rollout: a parallel run with reconciliation sign-off before legacy retirement.

real_life_risks: R1 [High | Integration dependencies] The 6 planned interfaces (knowledge base, e-commerce platform and telephony platform) are owned by different teams; the owner of knowledge base changes an API contract two weeks before UAT and the nightly sync for Professional services - knowledge article management starts failing without a clear owner. Indicative impact if unmanaged: 1–2 weeks of delay.

R2 [High | Data migration] After go-live of the pilot group, users of Professional services - knowledge article management find historical records missing or attached to the wrong customer, because the conversion of 32,000 records from older Dynamics 365 instance was only checked on a sample. Indicative impact if unmanaged: 1–2 weeks of delay.

R3 [High | Availability & performance] A failover test two weeks before go-live shows that recovery of Professional services - knowledge article management takes far longer than the agreed objectives, and the infrastructure team needs another environment cycle to fix it. Indicative impact if unmanaged: 1–2 weeks of delay.

R4 [Medium | Phased rollout & coexistence] The pilot of Professional services - knowledge article management goes well, but lessons from it (changed fields, new validation rules) arrive after the next wave's training material is produced, so later groups receive outdated guidance. Indicative impact if unmanaged: 1–2 weeks of delay.

R5 [Medium | Data quality & reporting trust] The first dashboards of Professional services - knowledge article management show numbers that differ from finance and operations reports, because source feeds are late or defined differently, and leaders stop trusting the data. Indicative impact if unmanaged: 1–2 weeks of delay.
risk_mitigation: M1 (Integration dependencies): Make every interface idempotent with retry and dead-letter handling, add integration monitoring that alerts on lag or failures, and schedule a joint end-to-end test with knowledge base and e-commerce platform before UAT begins.

M2 (Data migration): Migrate in prioritised waves (open items first, history last), keep the source system read-only but reachable for a fixed period, and publish a daily load-quality scorecard to the business owners.

M3 (Availability & performance): Rehearse failover and restore at least once, document recovery objectives and runbooks, and add monitoring with alerting thresholds tied to the 99.9% availability target.
M4 (Phased rollout & coexistence): Plan waves with fixed capacity for data load, access and support, keep a standing wave-readiness review, and protect the team from overlapping waves.
M5 (Data quality & reporting trust): Monitor freshness and row counts with alerts, quarantine bad records instead of dropping them, and publish known data issues alongside reports.
duration_reasoning: The model estimates 18 weeks (about 4.1 months) with a peak team of 17: 7 developers, 4 QA, 2 business analysts, 1 infrastructure, plus 1 project manager, 1 solution architect and 1 delivery lead. Indicative phase split (phases overlap in practice; the split sums to 18): discovery and design 2, build and configuration 5, integration and data work 5, testing and UAT 4, cutover and hypercare 2. Time drivers: (1) the 6 integrations (knowledge base, e-commerce platform and telephony platform) add specification, sandbox-wait and end-to-end test effort that does not shrink by adding developers; (2) moving 32,000 records from older Dynamics 365 instance needs profiling, mapping, cleansing and repeated trial loads, which is why the data work takes roughly 5 weeks of the plan; (3) the 99.9% availability target and the load from 709 named users require environment sizing, load testing and a failover rehearsal that must complete before go-live. Staffing rationale: 7 developers cover 6 scope areas (for example review workflow and search analytics) and 6 integrations; the pool is moderate because the scope offers limited parallel streams. 4 QA engineers are sized for control and compliance evidence, reconciliation checks and end-to-end integration regression. 1 infrastructure engineer handle environments, the 99.9% availability target, data-load runs and cutover support. Schedule sensitivity: if the 'Integration dependencies' risk is not contained, 1–2 weeks of slippage is realistic, so it is reviewed weekly.

Scope: plan changes; renewal tasks; work order types; job completion forms; user acceptance testing; operational runbooks. Integrations: e-signature service, telephony platform, data warehouse, document management system, knowledge base, calendar service. Data: migrate about 31,000 records from a legacy on-premises CRM. Non-functional needs: performance for 2745 named users, 99.5% availability target. Rollout: a single cutover weekend.

real_life_risks: R1 [High | Integration dependencies] A sandbox for e-signature service is not available until halfway through the build, so Telecommunications - subscription account management is developed against mocks and the first real end-to-end run exposes field-format and authentication problems. Indicative impact if unmanaged: 1–2 weeks of delay.

R2 [High | Big-bang cutover] A defect found in the first hour after cutover of Telecommunications - subscription account management cannot be fixed quickly, and because there is no pilot group the whole user base is affected at once. Indicative impact if unmanaged: 1–2 weeks of delay.

R3 [High | Data migration] After go-live of the pilot group, users of Telecommunications - subscription account management find historical records missing or attached to the wrong customer, because the conversion of 31,000 records from legacy on-premises CRM was only checked on a sample. Indicative impact if unmanaged: 1–2 weeks of delay.

R4 [High | Availability & performance] A failover test two weeks before go-live shows that recovery of Telecommunications - subscription account management takes far longer than the agreed objectives, and the infrastructure team needs another environment cycle to fix it. Indicative impact if unmanaged: 1–2 weeks of delay.

R5 [Medium | Key-person & skills dependency] The only developer who understands the customisations on Salesforce for Telecommunications - subscription account management falls ill or is moved to another project in the middle of the build, and nobody else can safely change that area. Indicative impact if unmanaged: 1–2 weeks of delay.
risk_mitigation: M1 (Integration dependencies): Make every interface idempotent with retry and dead-letter handling, add integration monitoring that alerts on lag or failures, and schedule a joint end-to-end test with e-signature service and telephony platform before UAT begins.

M2 (Big-bang cutover): Freeze changes and the legacy data one week before cutover, staff a command centre with developers, data and business leads for the first 72 hours, and pre-approve a rollback decision-maker.

M3 (Data migration): Migrate in prioritised waves (open items first, history last), keep the source system read-only but reachable for a fixed period, and publish a daily load-quality scorecard to the business owners.

M4 (Availability & performance): Schedule heavy batch work outside business peaks, use queue-based load levelling for integrations, and agree a capacity plan with the infrastructure owner before cutover.

M5 (Key-person & skills dependency): Pair developers on critical components, keep design decisions in a shared log and code in a reviewed repository, and nominate a named backup for the architect and delivery lead.
duration_reasoning: The model estimates 17 weeks (about 3.9 months) with a peak team of 18: 7 developers, 5 QA, 2 business analysts, 1 infrastructure, plus 1 project manager, 1 solution architect and 1 delivery lead. Indicative phase split (phases overlap in practice; the split sums to 17): discovery and design 2, build and configuration 5, integration and data work 4, testing and UAT 3, cutover and hypercare 3. Time drivers: (1) the 6 integrations (e-signature service, telephony platform and data warehouse) add specification, sandbox-wait and end-to-end test effort that does not shrink by adding developers; (2) a single cutover leaves no room for a staged fix, so the plan keeps extra time for dress rehearsals, rollback preparation and hypercare; (3) the conversion of 31,000 records from legacy on-premises CRM cannot be rushed because every trial load must be reconciled before UAT can start. Staffing rationale: 7 developers cover 6 scope areas (for example plan changes and renewal tasks) and 6 integrations; the pool is moderate because the scope offers limited parallel streams. 5 QA engineers are sized for performance and UAT support for a large user base and end-to-end integration regression. 1 infrastructure engineer handle environments, the 99.5% availability target, data-load runs and cutover support. Schedule sensitivity: if the 'Integration dependencies' risk is not contained, 1–2 weeks of slippage is realistic, so it is reviewed weekly.

real_life_risks: R1 [High | Big-bang cutover] The single cutover for Retail banking - chatbot virtual agent overruns its weekend window because the final data load takes longer than rehearsed; on Monday morning staff cannot work in either the old or the new system. Indicative impact if unmanaged: 1–2 weeks of delay.

R2 [High | Integration dependencies] A sandbox for document management system is not available until halfway through the build, so Retail banking - chatbot virtual agent is developed against mocks and the first real end-to-end run exposes field-format and authentication problems. risk_mitigation: M1 (Big-bang cutover): Hold at least two full dress rehearsals with timings, define a written rollback point and rollback test, and agree measurable go/no-go criteria with the business owner two weeks ahead.

M2 (Integration dependencies): Agree interface contracts and test accounts for each of the 4 integrations in the first sprints, build contract tests plus mocks so work is not blocked, and name one accountable owner per interface with a response-time agreement.

M3 (AI answer quality & knowledge): Assign owners and review dates for every knowledge article, add a feedback button on each answer, and measure resolution and escalation rates rather than demo performance.

M4 (Availability & performance): Rehearse failover and restore at least once, document recovery objectives and runbooks, and add monitoring with alerting thresholds tied to the 99.9% availability target.
duration_reasoning: The model estimates 12 weeks (about 2.8 months) with a peak team of 14: 5 developers, 2 QA, 2 business analysts, 2 infrastructure, plus 1 project manager, 1 solution architect and 1 delivery lead. Time drivers: (1) a single cutover leaves no room for a staged fix, so the plan keeps extra time for dress rehearsals, rollback preparation and hypercare; (2) connecting document management system, data warehouse and billing platform means 4 interfaces that must each be specified, built against third-party schedules and tested end to end; (3) AI and knowledge features need an evaluation set, content clean-up and tuning cycles that run alongside normal build work. Staffing rationale: 5 developers cover 3 scope areas (for example conversation logging and intent catalogue) and 4 integrations; the pool is moderate because the scope offers limited parallel streams. 2 QA engineers are sized for end-to-end integration regression. 2 infrastructure engineers handle environments, the 99.9% availability target, data-load runs and cutover support. Scope: photo capture; sync conflict handling; offline forms; audit history; operational runbooks; data validation rules. Integrations: ITSM tool, telephony platform, data warehouse, billing platform, SMS gateway, email gateway. Data: migrate about 4,000,000 records from a Salesforce org. Non-functional needs: performance for 1041 named users, 99.5% availability target. Rollout: a parallel run with reconciliation sign-off before legacy retirement.

real_life_risks: R1 [High | Data migration] During the second trial load of 4,000,000 records from Salesforce org, a share of them fail mapping because of orphaned parent IDs and conflicting duplicates, so Media company - mobile field app cannot be signed off for UAT on the planned date. Indicative impact if unmanaged: 1–3 weeks of delay.

R2 [High | Integration dependencies] The 6 planned interfaces (ITSM tool, telephony platform and data warehouse) are owned by different teams; the owner of ITSM tool changes an API contract two weeks before UAT and the nightly sync for Media company - mobile field app starts failing without a clear owner. Indicative impact if unmanaged: 1–2 weeks of delay.

R3 [High | Offline use & data sync] A new phone model or operating-system update breaks the offline cache of Media company - mobile field app, and technicians lose a day of captured photos and notes. Indicative impact if unmanaged: 1–2 weeks of delay.

R4 [Medium | Availability & performance] A failover test two weeks before go-live shows that recovery of Media company - mobile field app takes far longer than the agreed objectives, and the infrastructure team needs another environment cycle to fix it. Indicative impact if unmanaged: 1–2 weeks of delay.

R5 [Medium | Phased rollout & coexistence] The pilot of Media company - mobile field app goes well, but lessons from it (changed fields, new validation rules) arrive after the next wave's training material is produced, so later groups receive outdated guidance. Indicative impact if unmanaged: 1–2 weeks of delay.
risk_mitigation: M1 (Data migration): Migrate in prioritised waves (open items first, history last), keep the source system read-only but reachable for a fixed period, and publish a daily load-quality scorecard to the business owners.

M2 (Integration dependencies): Make every interface idempotent with retry and dead-letter handling, add integration monitoring that alerts on lag or failures, and schedule a joint end-to-end test with ITSM tool and telephony platform before UAT begins.
M3 (Offline use & data sync): Define explicit conflict-resolution rules, test sync on throttled and intermittent networks, and keep payloads small by syncing only what each role needs.

M4 (Availability & performance): Rehearse failover and restore at least once, document recovery objectives and runbooks, and add monitoring with alerting thresholds tied to the 99.5% availability target.

M5 (Phased rollout & coexistence): Turn pilot lessons into a controlled change list reviewed before each wave, update training material from one maintained source, and use readiness checklists per wave as an entry gate.
duration_reasoning: The model estimates 24 weeks (about 5.5 months) with a peak team of 24: 10 developers, 5 QA, 3 business analysts, 2 infrastructure, plus 1 project manager, 2 solution architects and 1 delivery lead. Indicative phase split (phases overlap in practice; the split sums to 24): discovery and design 3, build and configuration 7, integration and data work 6, testing and UAT 5, cutover and hypercare 3. Time drivers: (1) moving 4,000,000 records from Salesforce org needs profiling, mapping, cleansing and repeated trial loads, which is why the data work takes roughly 6 weeks of the plan; (2) connecting ITSM tool, telephony platform and data warehouse means 6 interfaces that must each be specified, built against third-party schedules and tested end to end; (3) offline and intermittent-connectivity behaviour needs conflict-handling design and device/network testing beyond normal functional QA. Staffing rationale: 10 developers cover 6 scope areas (for example photo capture and sync conflict handling) and 6 integrations; this is a larger pool because the work splits into parallel streams. 5 QA engineers are sized for control and compliance evidence, reconciliation checks and device and sync testing. 2 infrastructure engineers handle environments, the 99.5% availability target, data-load runs and cutover support. Schedule sensitivity: if the 'Data migration' risk is not contained, 1–3 weeks of slippage is realistic, so it is reviewed weekly.

Scope: row-level security; KPI glossary; data validation rules. Integrations: marketing automation platform, HR information system, master data service. Data: migrate about 6,000,000 records from an ERP customer table. Non-functional needs: performance for 4652 named users, 99.5% availability target. Rollout: a phased rollout by region.

real_life_risks: R1 [High | Data migration] Late in the build, data profiling of ERP customer table shows that 6,000,000 records carry inconsistent owners, missing mandatory fields and legacy codes nobody can explain, which stalls the load scripts for Financial services - data warehouse and BI reporting. Indicative impact if unmanaged: 1–2 weeks of delay.

R2 [High | Availability & performance] On the first peak day, Financial services - data warehouse and BI reporting slows down for 4,652 named users because queries and integrations were only tested with a fraction of the real volume, and the 99.5% availability target is missed. Indicative impact if unmanaged: 1–2 weeks of delay.

R3 [High | Integration dependencies] A sandbox for marketing automation platform is not available until halfway through the build, so Financial services - data warehouse and BI reporting is developed against mocks and the first real end-to-end run exposes field-format and authentication problems. Indicative impact if unmanaged: 1–2 weeks of delay.

R4 [Medium | Phased rollout & coexistence] Each wave of Financial services - data warehouse and BI reporting needs its own data load, access set-up and support cover, and a delay in one wave pushes the others and stretches the team's time on the project. Indicative impact if unmanaged: 1–2 weeks of delay.

R5 [Medium | User adoption & training] Training for Financial services - data warehouse and BI reporting is scheduled before the final design settles, so users learn screens that later change, and the service desk is flooded with how-do-I tickets in week one. Indicative impact if unmanaged: 1–2 weeks of delay.
risk_mitigation: M1 (Data migration): Profile and cleanse ERP customer table before build starts, run at least three timed trial loads with record-count and field-level reconciliation, and give a named data steward the authority to resolve conflicts within 48 hours.

M2 (Availability & performance): Run load tests at 1.5x expected peak with production-like data volumes, set performance budgets for key screens and integrations, and fix hotspots before UAT rather than after go-live.

M3 (Integration dependencies): Request sandbox access for marketing automation platform, HR information system and master data service during mobilisation, track it as a delivery milestone, and keep an interface risk log reviewed weekly by the solution architect.

M4 (Phased rollout & coexistence): Define which system is the source of truth per object for every wave, build a reconciliation report that runs daily during coexistence, and keep the coexistence period as short as the business accepts.
M5 (User adoption & training): Retire the old tools on a published date, collect early feedback through a short pulse survey, and fix the top friction points in a first post-go-live release.
duration_reasoning: The model estimates 22 weeks (about 5.1 months) with a peak team of 21: 8 developers, 4 QA, 3 business analysts, 2 infrastructure, plus 1 project manager, 2 solution architects and 1 delivery lead. Indicative phase split (phases overlap in practice; the split sums to 22): discovery and design 3, build and configuration 6, integration and data work 6, testing and UAT 4, cutover and hypercare 3. Time drivers: (1) moving 6,000,000 records from ERP customer table needs profiling, mapping, cleansing and repeated trial loads, which is why the data work takes roughly 6 weeks of the plan; (2) meeting 99.5% availability for 4,652 named users adds performance tuning cycles that sit in the test phase; (3) the 3 integrations (marketing automation platform, HR information system and master data service) add specification, sandbox-wait and end-to-end test effort that does not shrink by adding developers. Staffing rationale: 8 developers cover 3 scope areas (for example row-level security and KPI glossary) and 3 integrations; this is a larger pool because the work splits into parallel streams. 4 QA engineers are sized for performance and UAT support for a large user base. 2 infrastructure engineers handle environments, the 99.5% availability target, data-load runs and cutover support. Schedule sensitivity: if the 'Data migration' risk is not contained, 1–2 weeks of slippage is realistic, so it is reviewed weekly.

Scope: export controls; drill-through paths; scheduled alerts; release approvals; automated tests; reviewer feedback; confidence thresholds; breach notifications; entitlement lookup; user acceptance testing; Teams or Outlook notifications; security roles and row-level access. Integrations: e-signature service, data warehouse, identity provider for single sign-on, telematics feed, document management system, survey platform. Data: no migration. Non-functional needs: performance for 2448 named users, 99.9% availability target. Rollout: a parallel run with reconciliation sign-off before legacy retirement.

real_life_risks: R1 [High | Integration dependencies] A sandbox for e-signature service is not available until halfway through the build, so Hospitality - analytics dashboard release is developed against mocks and the first real end-to-end run exposes field-format and authentication problems. Indicative impact if unmanaged: 1–3 weeks of delay.

R2 [High | Availability & performance] On the first peak day, Hospitality - analytics dashboard release slows down for 2,448 named users because queries and integrations were only tested with a fraction of the real volume, and the 99.9% availability target is missed. Indicative impact if unmanaged: 1–3 weeks of delay.

R3 [Medium | Scope growth] A senior stakeholder asks for an extra capability late in the project, and without a change process the team quietly absorbs it, eroding the testing time reserved for Hospitality - analytics dashboard release. Indicative impact if unmanaged: 1–3 weeks of delay.

R4 [High | Phased rollout & coexistence] Each wave of Hospitality - analytics dashboard release needs its own data load, access set-up and support cover, and a delay in one wave pushes the others and stretches the team's time on the project. Indicative impact if unmanaged: 1–3 weeks of delay.

R5 [Medium | Data quality & reporting trust] Two departments argue over the definition of a key measure in Hospitality - analytics dashboard release, so metric sign-off is delayed and dashboards are rebuilt twice. Indicative impact if unmanaged: 1–3 weeks of delay.
risk_mitigation: M1 (Integration dependencies): Make every interface idempotent with retry and dead-letter handling, add integration monitoring that alerts on lag or failures, and schedule a joint end-to-end test with e-signature service and data warehouse before UAT begins.

M2 (Availability & performance): Run load tests at 1.5x expected peak with production-like data volumes, set performance budgets for key screens and integrations, and fix hotspots before UAT rather than after go-live.

M3 (Scope growth): Hold early design workshops with written acceptance criteria per capability, demo every sprint to the same decision-makers, and log any new request as a change with an explicit trade-off.
M4 (Phased rollout & coexistence): Plan waves with fixed capacity for data load, access and support, keep a standing wave-readiness review, and protect the team from overlapping waves.
M5 (Data quality & reporting trust): Monitor freshness and row counts with alerts, quarantine bad records instead of dropping them, and publish known data issues alongside reports.
duration_reasoning: The model estimates 32 weeks (about 7.4 months) with a peak team of 26: 10 developers, 5 QA, 4 business analysts, 2 infrastructure, plus 1 project manager, 2 solution architects and 2 delivery leads. Indicative phase split (phases overlap in practice; the split sums to 32): discovery and design 5, build and configuration 9, integration and data work 7, testing and UAT 7, cutover and hypercare 4. Time drivers: (1) the 6 integrations (e-signature service, data warehouse and identity provider for single sign-on) add specification, sandbox-wait and end-to-end test effort that does not shrink by adding developers; (2) meeting 99.9% availability for 2,448 named users adds performance tuning cycles that sit in the test phase; (3) the scope covers 13 capability areas such as export controls and drill-through paths, and each one needs design, build and acceptance testing. Staffing rationale: 10 developers cover 13 scope areas (for example export controls and drill-through paths) and 6 integrations; this is a larger pool because the work splits into parallel streams. 5 QA engineers are sized for reconciliation checks, performance and UAT support for a large user base and end-to-end integration regression. 2 infrastructure engineers handle environments, the 99.9% availability target, data-load runs and cutover support. real_life_risks: R1 [High | Data migration] After go-live of the pilot group, users of Insurance - quote and approval workflow find historical records missing or attached to the wrong customer, because the conversion of 354,000 records from homegrown database was only checked on a sample. R2 [High | Big-bang cutover] The single cutover for Insurance - quote and approval workflow overruns its weekend window because the final data load takes longer than rehearsed; on Monday morning staff cannot work in either the old or the new system. R3 [High | Integration dependencies] In UAT, messages between marketing automation platform and ITSM tool arrive late or twice, causing duplicate updates and stale records in Insurance - quote and approval workflow that business testers cannot reconcile by hand. Indicative impact if unmanaged: 1–2 weeks of delay.

R4 [Medium | Availability & performance] A failover test two weeks before go-live shows that recovery of Insurance - quote and approval workflow takes far longer than the agreed objectives, and the infrastructure team needs another environment cycle to fix it. M2 (Big-bang cutover): Where possible reduce blast radius by switching low-risk groups first or running read-only in parallel for a day, and prepare short user guides for the likely first-day issues.

M3 (Integration dependencies): Agree interface contracts and test accounts for each of the 4 integrations in the first sprints, build contract tests plus mocks so work is not blocked, and name one accountable owner per interface with a response-time agreement.

M4 (Availability & performance): Rehearse failover and restore at least once, document recovery objectives and runbooks, and add monitoring with alerting thresholds tied to the 99.5% availability target.
