Scope: reopen handling; ticket categories; auto-acknowledgement; assignment rules; product configuration; discount authority; audit history; Power Automate notifications; security roles and row-level access. Integrations: learning management system, email gateway, document management system, telematics feed, legacy CRM, HR information system. Data: migrate about 2,000,000 records from an older Dynamics 365 instance. Non-functional needs: performance for 700 named users, 99.9% availability target; segregation of duties for approvals. Rollout: a ring-based deployment with feature flags.

real_life_risks: R1 [High | Data migration] During the second trial load of 2,000,000 records from older Dynamics 365 instance, a share of them fail mapping because of orphaned parent IDs and conflicting duplicates, so Retail banking - helpdesk ticket routing cannot be signed off for UAT on the planned date. Indicative impact if unmanaged: 1–3 weeks of delay.

R2 [High | Integration dependencies] A sandbox for learning management system is not available until halfway through the build, so Retail banking - helpdesk ticket routing is developed against mocks and the first real end-to-end run exposes field-format and authentication problems. Indicative impact if unmanaged: 1–3 weeks of delay.

R3 [High | Availability & performance] On the first peak day, Retail banking - helpdesk ticket routing slows down for 700 named users because queries and integrations were only tested with a fraction of the real volume, and the 99.9% availability target is missed. Indicative impact if unmanaged: 1–2 weeks of delay.

R4 [High | Security & compliance] The auditor asks for evidence that segregation-of-duties controls, audit-trail requirements and role-based and row-level access is enforced end to end, but the logs and approval trails in Retail banking - helpdesk ticket routing were never designed to be exported, so release is paused. Indicative impact if unmanaged: 1–3 weeks of delay.

R5 [Medium | Device & telemetry reliability] A network outage creates a backlog of device messages; when connectivity returns the burst overloads the ingestion layer of Retail banking - helpdesk ticket routing and real alarms are delayed. Indicative impact if unmanaged: 1–2 weeks of delay.
risk_mitigation: M1 (Data migration): Profile and cleanse older Dynamics 365 instance before build starts, run at least three timed trial loads with record-count and field-level reconciliation, and give a named data steward the authority to resolve conflicts within 48 hours.

M2 (Integration dependencies): Request sandbox access for learning management system, email gateway and document management system during mobilisation, track it as a delivery milestone, and keep an interface risk log reviewed weekly by the solution architect.

M3 (Availability & performance): Schedule heavy batch work outside business peaks, use queue-based load levelling for integrations, and agree a capacity plan with the infrastructure owner before cutover.

M4 (Security & compliance): Run a threat-model and control-mapping workshop in the first month, make each control in segregation-of-duties controls, audit-trail requirements and role-based and row-level access a Definition-of-Done item, and test with negative cases (users who should be blocked) in every sprint.
M5 (Device & telemetry reliability): Design ingestion with buffering, back-pressure and replay, and load-test burst scenarios that are several times the normal message rate.
duration_reasoning: The model estimates 26 weeks (about 6.0 months) with a peak team of 25: 10 developers, 5 QA, 3 business analysts, 3 infrastructure, plus 1 project manager, 2 solution architects and 1 delivery lead. Indicative phase split (phases overlap in practice; the split sums to 26): discovery and design 3, build and configuration 7, integration and data work 7, testing and UAT 6, cutover and hypercare 3. Time drivers: (1) the conversion of 2,000,000 records from older Dynamics 365 instance cannot be rushed because every trial load must be reconciled before UAT can start; (2) the 6 integrations (learning management system, email gateway and document management system) add specification, sandbox-wait and end-to-end test effort that does not shrink by adding developers; (3) the 99.9% availability target and the load from 700 named users require environment sizing, load testing and a failover rehearsal that must complete before go-live. Staffing rationale: 10 developers cover 10 scope areas (for example reopen handling and ticket categories) and 6 integrations; this is a larger pool because the work splits into parallel streams. 5 QA engineers are sized for control and compliance evidence and end-to-end integration regression. 3 infrastructure engineers handle environments, the 99.9% availability target, data-load runs and cutover support. Schedule sensitivity: if the 'Data migration' risk is not contained, 1–3 weeks of slippage is realistic, so it is reviewed weekly.

real_life_risks: R1 [High | Data migration] Late in the build, data profiling of homegrown database shows that 591,000 records carry inconsistent owners, missing mandatory fields and legacy codes nobody can explain, which stalls the load scripts for Wholesale distribution - data warehouse and BI reporting. Indicative impact if unmanaged: 1–2 weeks of delay.

R2 [High | Availability & performance] A background batch job and user traffic compete for the same resources at month-end, and Wholesale distribution - data warehouse and BI reporting becomes unresponsive exactly when 1,840 named users need it most. Indicative impact if unmanaged: 1–2 weeks of delay.

R3 [Medium | Integration dependencies] The 3 planned interfaces (master data service, calendar service and learning management system) are owned by different teams; the owner of master data service changes an API contract two weeks before UAT and the nightly sync for Wholesale distribution - data warehouse and BI reporting starts failing without a clear owner. Indicative impact if unmanaged: 1–2 weeks of delay.

R4 [Medium | User adoption & training] After go-live of Wholesale distribution - data warehouse and BI reporting, 1,840 named users keep using the old spreadsheets and email threads for edge cases because the new flows feel slower, so the data in Wholesale distribution - data warehouse and BI reporting stays incomplete and benefits are not seen. Indicative impact if unmanaged: 1–2 weeks of delay.

R5 [Medium | Phased rollout & coexistence] During the rollout of Wholesale distribution - data warehouse and BI reporting (a pilot with two business units followed by regional rollout), the old and new systems both hold live data; users in the first wave update one system while later waves use the other, and managers see two versions of the truth. Indicative impact if unmanaged: 1–2 weeks of delay.
risk_mitigation: M1 (Data migration): Profile and cleanse homegrown database before build starts, run at least three timed trial loads with record-count and field-level reconciliation, and give a named data steward the authority to resolve conflicts within 48 hours.

M2 (Availability & performance): Schedule heavy batch work outside business peaks, use queue-based load levelling for integrations, and agree a capacity plan with the infrastructure owner before cutover.

M3 (Integration dependencies): Request sandbox access for master data service, calendar service and learning management system during mobilisation, track it as a delivery milestone, and keep an interface risk log reviewed weekly by the solution architect.
M4 (User adoption & training): Track adoption KPIs (active users, records created, old-tool usage) weekly after go-live, and have leaders review them in team meetings until usage stabilises.

M5 (Phased rollout & coexistence): Define which system is the source of truth per object for every wave, build a reconciliation report that runs daily during coexistence, and keep the coexistence period as short as the business accepts.
duration_reasoning: The model estimates 17 weeks (about 3.9 months) with a peak team of 17: 7 developers, 4 QA, 2 business analysts, 1 infrastructure, plus 1 project manager, 1 solution architect and 1 delivery lead. Indicative phase split (phases overlap in practice; the split sums to 17): discovery and design 2, build and configuration 5, integration and data work 4, testing and UAT 4, cutover and hypercare 2. Time drivers: (1) the conversion of 591,000 records from homegrown database cannot be rushed because every trial load must be reconciled before UAT can start; (2) meeting 99.9% availability for 1,840 named users adds performance tuning cycles that sit in the test phase; (3) connecting master data service, calendar service and learning management system means 3 interfaces that must each be specified, built against third-party schedules and tested end to end. Staffing rationale: 7 developers cover 9 scope areas (for example scheduled refresh and row-level security) and 3 integrations; the pool is moderate because the scope offers limited parallel streams. 4 QA engineers are sized for performance and UAT support for a large user base. 1 infrastructure engineer handle environments, the 99.9% availability target, data-load runs and cutover support. Indicative impact if unmanaged: 1–2 weeks of delay.

R2 [High | Availability & performance] A background batch job and user traffic compete for the same resources at month-end, and Logistics and freight - CI/CD release pipeline becomes unresponsive exactly when 1,412 named users need it most. Indicative impact if unmanaged: 1–2 weeks of delay.

R3 [High | Integration dependencies] A sandbox for ITSM tool is not available until halfway through the build, so Logistics and freight - CI/CD release pipeline is developed against mocks and the first real end-to-end run exposes field-format and authentication problems. Indicative impact if unmanaged: 1–2 weeks of delay.

R4 [Medium | Key-person & skills dependency] The solution architect becomes a bottleneck because every design question for Logistics and freight - CI/CD release pipeline waits for one person, so developers idle or build on assumptions that later change. Indicative impact if unmanaged: 1–2 weeks of delay.

R5 [Medium | Phased rollout & coexistence] During the rollout of Logistics and freight - CI/CD release pipeline (a pilot with two business units followed by regional rollout), the old and new systems both hold live data; users in the first wave update one system while later waves use the other, and managers see two versions of the truth. Indicative impact if unmanaged: 1–2 weeks of delay.
risk_mitigation: M1 (Data migration): Profile and cleanse Salesforce org before build starts, run at least three timed trial loads with record-count and field-level reconciliation, and give a named data steward the authority to resolve conflicts within 48 hours.

M2 (Availability & performance): Run load tests at 1.5x expected peak with production-like data volumes, set performance budgets for key screens and integrations, and fix hotspots before UAT rather than after go-live.

M3 (Integration dependencies): Agree interface contracts and test accounts for each of the 5 integrations in the first sprints, build contract tests plus mocks so work is not blocked, and name one accountable owner per interface with a response-time agreement.
M4 (Key-person & skills dependency): Document the build as you go (runbooks, configuration notes) so a replacement can be productive within days rather than weeks.

M5 (Phased rollout & coexistence): Define which system is the source of truth per object for every wave, build a reconciliation report that runs daily during coexistence, and keep the coexistence period as short as the business accepts.
duration_reasoning: The model estimates 17 weeks (about 3.9 months) with a peak team of 18: 8 developers, 4 QA, 2 business analysts, 1 infrastructure, plus 1 project manager, 1 solution architect and 1 delivery lead. Indicative phase split (phases overlap in practice; the split sums to 17): discovery and design 2, build and configuration 5, integration and data work 4, testing and UAT 4, cutover and hypercare 2. Time drivers: (1) the conversion of 326,000 records from Salesforce org cannot be rushed because every trial load must be reconciled before UAT can start; (2) meeting 99.9% availability for 1,412 named users adds performance tuning cycles that sit in the test phase; (3) the 5 integrations (ITSM tool, email gateway and telephony platform) add specification, sandbox-wait and end-to-end test effort that does not shrink by adding developers. Staffing rationale: 8 developers cover 5 scope areas (for example automated tests and release approvals) and 5 integrations; this is a larger pool because the work splits into parallel streams. 4 QA engineers are sized for control and compliance evidence, performance and UAT support for a large user base and end-to-end integration regression. 1 infrastructure engineer handle environments, the 99.9% availability target, data-load runs and cutover support. Schedule sensitivity: if the 'Data migration' risk is not contained, 1–2 weeks of slippage is realistic, so it is reviewed weekly.
